query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a modest aluminum addition to the refractory high‐entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in situ formation of a continuous, protective alumina scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy with a base composition similar to W–Ta–V–Cr that currently does not form a protective oxide layer at extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: Add a minor amount of aluminum (via surface alloying or bulk modification) to the refractory HEA composition.
generation.conditions: Exposing the alloy to an oxygen‐rich atmosphere (e.g., air) at temperatures between 1000°C and 1200°C for extended durations (e.g., 50 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Upon high-temperature exposure, aluminum segregates to the surface and oxidizes preferentially to form a slow-growing, dense alumina barrier. This oxide layer impedes further oxygen penetration, thereby reducing the oxidation of the underlying refractory HEA.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated alloys, the aluminum-modified alloy will exhibit a significantly reduced oxide scale thickness and lower oxidation kinetics, leading to enhanced mechanical stability under extreme-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Refractory HEA samples without aluminum addition, which under similar high-temperature and oxygen-rich conditions develop thicker, less protective oxide scales.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when the aluminum content is optimized: too little may not form an effective oxide layer, while too much might lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases or non-protective oxide morphologies. The hypothesis is also limited to the temperature regime (approximately 1000°C–1200°C) where alumina formation kinetics and adhesion are favorable.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., percentage reduction in oxide thickness or oxidation kinetics) is uncertain and likely sensitive to the aluminum concentration and processing route. Long-term cyclic thermal exposures might also affect the stability of the alumina layer, which requires further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA specimens with a base W–Ta–V–Cr composition. One set will receive a controlled aluminum addition (via surface treatment or alloying) while the control set remains untreated. Expose both sets to air at 1100°C for 50 hours.
measurements: Measure the oxide scale thickness using SEM/TEM and determine its composition using EDS or XPS.
Record mass gain to compare oxidation kinetics.
Perform mechanical property evaluation (e.g., nanoindentation) to assess any corresponding improvement in structural integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale thickness, lower mass gain, or improved mechanical performance compared to the untreated control, then the hypothesis that aluminum addition improves high-temperature oxygen resistance is falsified.

System: Quaternary W-Ta-V-Cr high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V. Processing: Magnetron sputtering deposition from pure metal targets (99.99% purity) using powers of 192 W (Cr), 312 W (V), 277 W (Ta), and 300 W (W) at 3 mtorr pressure and room temperature; films deposited on NaCl (100 nm) or Si (3 μm) substrates.
